question.prompt: Kayla rolls four fair \(6\)-sided dice. What is the probability that at least one of the numbers Kayla rolls is greater than \(4\) and at least two of the numbers she rolls are greater than \(2?\)

solutions.title: Subtract disjoint failure cases
solutions.explanation:
A roll greater than \(4\) already supplies one number greater than \(2\). This makes it easy to describe exactly how the requirements can fail.

There are two disjoint failure cases:

1. No die shows a number greater than \(4\). Each die must show one of \(1,2,3,4\), so independence gives probability
\[
\left(\frac46\right)^4=\frac{16}{81}.
\]
2. At least one die shows a number greater than \(4\), but fewer than two dice show numbers greater than \(2\). This means exactly one die shows \(5\) or \(6\), and the other three show \(1\) or \(2\). There are four choices for the exceptional die, giving probability
\[
4\left(\frac26\right)\left(\frac26\right)^3=\frac4{81}.
\]

Every failure belongs to one of these cases, and they cannot overlap because only the second contains a roll greater than \(4\). Therefore the desired probability is
\[
1-\frac{16}{81}-\frac4{81}=\boxed{\frac{61}{81}},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

solutions.title: Count by the number of high rolls
solutions.explanation:
Only three categories matter: low \(\{1,2\}\), middle \(\{3,4\}\), and high \(\{5,6\}\). Each category has probability \(1/3\), so the \(3^4=81\) ordered category patterns are equally likely.

Count successful patterns by the number \(k\) of high dice. If \(k\ge2\), both requirements hold automatically. Choose the high positions in \(\binom4k\) ways; each remaining position can be low or middle, giving \(2^{4-k}\) possibilities.

If \(k=1\), choose the high position in four ways. The remaining three positions may be low or middle, but they cannot all be low: at least one must supply the second number greater than \(2\).

| Number of high dice | Successful patterns |
|---|---:|
| \(1\) | \(4(2^3-1)=28\) |
| \(2\) | \(\binom42 2^2=24\) |
| \(3\) | \(\binom43 2=8\) |
| \(4\) | \(1\) |

These cases include every successful pattern exactly once, since each pattern has a unique number of high dice. Thus the probability is
\[
\frac{28+24+8+1}{81}=\boxed{\frac{61}{81}},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
